**Q2. Community composition: what structures it more, climate or disturbance?**

Hypotheses:

1. Rainfall and dry-season length set the main floristic turnover (evergreen → deciduous forest).
2. Disturbance shifts plots toward deciduous and non-endemic species.

## 1. Load clean data

The raw files were checked and cleaned in `01_Data_Cleaning.Rmd`.

```{r q2-load-data}
load("Data/clean/clean_data.RData", verbose = TRUE)

# All tables have the plots in the same order
stopifnot(identical(rownames(comm_macro), env$PlotID))
```
## 2. Transforming the community data

Abundances are skewed (few very common species, many rare ones), so we use a
log(x+1) transformation, as in class.

```{r q2-transform}
hist(comm_macro[comm_macro > 0])          # raw abundances
hist(log1p(comm_macro[comm_macro > 0]))   # log(x+1)

comm_log <- log1p(comm_macro)
```

## 3. Community dissimilarity and clustering

### 3.1 Bray-Curtis distance and hierarchical clustering

Bray-Curtis is bounded between 0 and 1 and does not count shared absences as
similarity, which suits species-rich data with many zeros.

```{r q2-cluster}
vd <- vegdist(comm_log, "bray")

o.clu <- hclust(vd, method = "ward.D2")   # Ward: minimises variance within clusters
plot(as.dendrogram(o.clu), leaflab = "none", main = "Ward clustering (Bray-Curtis)")
```
DCA for gradient length, which justifies RDA vs CCA for P4. NMDS (Bray–Curtis) with envfit/ordisurf (e.g. a rainfall surface).
Cluster analysis (hclust, cutree) on Bray–Curtis or Hellinger distances; compare the clusters with ForestType and use envfit species vectors to see which species characterise them. 
PERMANOVA (adonis2) by disturbance and forest type, with betadisper to check dispersion
